title: The Margins We Leave Open
subtitle: A Lanternweald continuation
content:
The trouble began with a note written in the wrong ink.

There were plenty of things to dislike about the Moonroot Archive. The stairs to the upper gallery were narrow. The newest shelving unit leaned half an inch to the left. Someone had cataloged a book of medicinal fungi under local legends because its cover showed a dragon.

Severus had written three complaints about that last offense.

The note was worse.

I found it between pages sixty-eight and sixty-nine of a borrowed potions manual. The handwriting was neat and small, slanted toward the gutter as though the writer had been trying to fit the whole world into the margins.

At first I thought it was a correction.

Then I read the instructions.

My stomach tightened.

"Severus?"

He was at the reference desk sorting returned volumes into piles he refused to call piles.

"If you have discovered another misfiled cookbook, I would prefer the information in writing."

"Come look at this."

He heard something in my voice. By the time I looked up, he was already walking toward me.

I handed him the open book. He read the first two lines, then took out his wand and shut the volume with a quiet, exact motion.

"Don't touch that page again."

"I wasn't planning to lick it."

"Your usual standards for self-preservation are inconsistent."

He turned the book so its spine faced away from us and examined the ink through the thin paper.

"That is not merely incorrect," he said. "Someone altered the catalyst ratio. The mixture would become volatile long before it reached the claimed temperature."

"Accident or sabotage?"

"I don't know."

It was probably the first time he had said those words before exhausting every possible route to a different answer. I noticed. He noticed me noticing.

"Do not look so pleased."

"I'm relieved you didn't pretend."

He stared for a moment, then went back to the book.

Neri arrived carrying the borrowing ledger. Their walking stick tapped twice against the floor.

"Problem?" they asked.

Severus did not soften his answer.

"Yes."

Neri looked at the sealed volume. "Can we remove the page?"

"No," I said, at the same moment Severus said, "Not until we know what else is written on it."

Neri glanced between us. "That sounded almost coordinated."

"An unfortunate coincidence," Severus said.

We took the book to the protected workroom and set it on a slate table. Through the window the Lanternwell was visible beyond the garden, its lights pale in the morning haze. Someone was laughing in the square. I was grateful the sound could reach us.

Severus tested the ink with a harmless reveal charm. The annotation did not move. It had been written with ordinary black ink over faint pencil marks.

"That's a relief," I said.

"Only if you were expecting the book to bite."

"I have met your books."

He ignored me.

The borrowing ledger showed four people had handled the manual during the previous week. One was a student studying general herb lore. One was a visiting healer. One was an apprentice trying to repair a damaged binding. The fourth had signed only an initial.

"Whoever wrote it had access," Neri said.

"That narrows it down to the people who could touch the book," I said.

Severus gave me the look he saved for bad experimental design.

"Your contribution is noted."

I made a second list anyway. Not names of suspects. Facts we could establish. The ink was dry. The pencil marks were older. The alteration sat over a recipe that had already been corrected in the published errata.

"Someone copied an older mistake," I said.

"Or chose it deliberately."

"Both possibilities belong on the page."

Severus paused.

He had spent enough years being judged by partial evidence to know the violence of a convenient conclusion. He also knew how dangerous a careless instruction could be. Watching him hold both truths at once felt like watching a blade being set down on a table, slowly, with the edge turned away.

"We can restrict the volume," Neri said.

"Temporarily," Severus answered.

"And then?"

"Then we make a clean teaching copy with the corrected recipe, an explanation of the error and a notice that the original is being examined."

I blinked.

He looked at me.

"What?"

"Nothing. I was expecting a demand to lock every book in the building forever."

"Do not mistake my dislike of incompetence for an enthusiasm for censorship."

"That's a very romantic distinction."

"Your standards remain alarming."

We spent the next three hours doing the kind of work no one would write a heroic ballad about. Severus compared formulas. Neri checked the archive's circulation rules. I wrote the notice, crossed out three phrases that sounded accusatory, and wrote it again.

At noon, the visiting healer came to the workroom with a worried expression.

"I saw the sign," she said. "I borrowed that manual."

"Then perhaps you can help us," I told her.

She looked at Severus's black robes and flinched.

He saw it.

"The question is whether you observed pencil marks when you used the volume," he said, not gently but without accusation.

"I did. I thought they were notes from the previous borrower."

"Did you use the amended recipe?"

"No." She lifted a small notebook. "I copied it, though."

The room went cold.

Severus asked her to open the notebook. She did. He pointed out the dangerous ratio, explained the correct sequence, and told her why the difference mattered. He did not speak as if she were foolish for nearly trusting the printed page.

When she left with a corrected copy, he remained by the door for a while.

"You're staring," he said.

"I am."

"You are becoming remarkably impolite."

"You were a good teacher."

His jaw tightened.

"That is a subject on which opinions have varied."

"I know."

He returned to the desk. "Then do not make it a monument."

"I wasn't planning to."

The apprentice arrived before closing. They admitted using the manual to repair the binding but had not touched the notes. Their hands shook as they told us. Neri offered them a chair.

That left one initial unaccounted for, and no grounds for a grand accusation. We placed the original under controlled access, posted the corrected recipe and arranged a review of the other manuals on the shelf.

The problem was contained, not solved.

At dusk I found Severus on the archive steps with the rejected notice in his hand.

"You left that in my office," he said.

I took the sheet. He had corrected two commas and underlined a sentence.

I HAD BELIEVED THE NOTES SAFE UNTIL THE EVIDENCE CHANGED.

"That's honest," I said.

"An uncomfortable quality, I am told."

I sat beside him. The stone held the day's warmth. From Starwake Pier came a faint guitar chord; somewhere in the square, Maui was complaining that a lantern hook was too short.

"You could go home if you wanted," I said. "You don't owe this place every evening."

"I am aware."

"Just checking."

He turned slightly.

"Are you attempting to dismiss me so that you may attend to your other commitments?"

"No. I'm asking whether you want to stay here with me."

"Ah."

He looked toward the arches. The lights were coming on one by one.

"Then yes," he said.

I put my hand on the step between us. He covered it with his, warm and spare and certain.

For a long time we watched the square fill with people returning from their days. No one asked Severus to become someone easier. No one asked me to turn a dangerous mistake into a tidy moral lesson.

When we finally stood, he offered me his arm.

"Shall we go home?" he asked.

"I thought you hated the stairwell."

"I do."

"And the shelving."

"An offense."

"And the catalog."

"A crime."

I tucked the corrected notice under my free arm.

"And yet?"

He glanced at me.

"There is work worth doing," he said. "And somebody must keep you from misplacing the punctuation."

We walked through the Moonroot Door together. The original book stayed locked away for the night.

The question of who had written in it remained open.

So did the door.
